title: The city with open gates (Revelation 21:9–27)
hookLine: the gates are never shut, and the nations bring their glory in

cards: What's a city wall for? Keeping danger out, and people safe after dark. When Nehemiah rebuilt Jerusalem's walls, he ordered that the gates not open until the sun was hot, and that the doors be shut and barred.
In today's passage an angel carries John to a great high mountain and shows him the holy Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven. It has a wall, great and high, and twelve gates, each a single pearl.
If you've heard of the pearly gates, here they are. And then one line turns the whole idea of a city wall inside out.

teach.h: TRIBES ON THE GATES, APOSTLES BELOW.
teach.b: First, the names. On the twelve gates are the names of the twelve tribes of the children of Israel; on the wall's twelve foundations, the twelve apostles of the Lamb. The city carries both.

teach.h: NO TEMPLE, NO NEED OF THE SUN.
teach.b: Second, what's missing: "And I saw no temple therein: for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of it." No need of sun or moon either: God's glory lights it, and the Lamb is its light.
No special holy building, because the whole place is near to God. Third, the gates: "And the gates of it shall not be shut at all by day: for there shall be no night there."
Never shut by day, in a city with no night: never shut. And look who walks in: "And they shall bring the glory and honour of the nations into it." The kings of the earth come carrying their glory.
Two chapters earlier, they gathered to make war against the rider on the white horse. Now they arrive at an open gate.
Isaiah had pictured something like it: Jerusalem's gates open continually, not shut day nor night, with the wealth of the nations brought in. Fourth, the edge.
Verse twenty-seven says nothing that defiles will enter, only those written in the Lamb's book of life. Christians read the open gates and that verse differently.
Some hear a welcome that reaches very wide; others, an open city with a clear standard. The chapter sets them side by side and lets both stand.

how: The phrase 'pearly gates' comes from the gates of pearl in Revelation 21:21, and some churches read the vision of the holy city at funerals and on feasts of dedication.

games.q: what does “the city with open gates” mean?
o: a church that keeps its doors unlocked all day
a walled town that bars its gates every night
the holy Jerusalem whose pearl gates never close

games.q: the holy city — tap the pairs.
p: the names of the twelve tribes
the names of the twelve apostles
the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb

s: Revelation puts Peter at the pearly gates
the text has pearl gates with the tribes' names on them; it doesn't place Peter there.
the holy city has no temple
"for the Lord God Almighty and the Lamb are the temple of it."
the city's gates are shut each night

games.q: you're a gate of the holy city. in Nehemiah's Jerusalem, gates stayed shut until the sun was hot. what does Revelation say about you?
o: you're shut and barred, and opened only when the sun is hot.
you're not shut at all by day, and there is no night.
games.why: "the gates of it shall not be shut at all by day: for there shall be no night there." never shut.

practice: If you can, open a door or a window and sit where you can see it, noticing the air that moves through and the sounds from the other side.
Bring to mind one person you've quietly closed a gate on, not someone who's a danger to you, just someone you stopped letting in, and without deciding anything, picture the gate standing open.
If you pray, bring their name; if not, just breathe by the open door.

wordCard.voice: The city with open gates. Revelation's holy Jerusalem: twelve gates of pearl, no temple, no night, and gates that are never shut.

orig.note: Greek: a gateway, a gate. the word for the twelve gates of the holy city.

carryVoice: Your line: the gates are never shut. No night, so no closing time. Until tomorrow.
